Before you begin Create a Project A collection holds functions and the tables they write. The group it is created in decides which kind of function it can hold, and that is fixed for the collection's life. A source or destination collection also carries exactly one connection, and it is created together with that connection rather than separately. Step 1Create a data product collection, for transformers tdk collection create \ --proj finance \ --name reporting \ --group default \ --description "Reporting tables" A collection in default, or in any group you created, holds transformers and takes no connection. Passing --conn-file here is an error. Step 2Or create a source collection, with its connection tdk collection create \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --group sources \ --conn-file conn-postgres.yaml --conn-file is required for sources and destinations. The CLI derives the group from the connection's direction, so --group acts as an assertion: a mismatch is an error rather than a preference. Step 3Confirm it exists tdk collection list --proj finance tdk collection get --proj finance --name sales_src tdk collection get prints a data product collection's type as Data Factory, which is the same thing the docs call a data product.

--storage-path is the logical prefix for the collection's artifacts, written as base_path in the API. Unset, it inherits the project's prefix, and the resolved value is readable as effective_base_path. Changing it later is not retroactive: existing data versions keep the path they were written under, and only new artifacts use the new prefix.

Register a function into the collection. A source collection takes publishers, a destination collection takes subscribers, and a data product collection takes transformers. See tdk collection create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Collection Deleting a collection deletes its functions and tables, and freezes functions elsewhere that read from it. It takes a typed confirmation. Step 1Check what depends on the collection tdk table list --proj finance --coll sales_src Functions in other collections that read these tables are frozen by the delete, so it is worth knowing which tables those are. Step 2Delete it tdk collection delete \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src --confirm takes the literal string delete.

The delete is a soft delete with a cascade, in this order: The collection row is renamed to deleted_<id>, which frees the original name for immediate reuse. Functions in other collections that depend on its tables are set to Frozen. A frozen function stays registered and stops running until it is re-registered against tables that exist. Its tables, triggers and dependencies are set to Deleted, and its own functions are set to Deleted. Scheduled cron and stage workers are stopped. After the commit, the connection's stored content is deleted on a best-effort basis. Function status is one of Active, Frozen or Deleted, so a frozen function is visible in a listing rather than silently gone. See tdk collection delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Collection tdk collection update changes a collection's name, its description, its storage path, or the connection it carries. What it cannot change is the collection's type or the group it belongs to: both are fixed at creation. Step 1Rename it, or change its description tdk collection update \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --new-name sales_source \ --description "Postgres sales tables" Renaming a source or destination collection renames its connection too, since the connection is named by the collection. Step 2Or replace the connection tdk collection update \ --proj finance \ --name sales_src \ --conn-file conn-postgres-prod.yaml The connector kind is fixed for the collection's life, so the replacement document has to be the same kind. Pointing a publisher at a different database means a new connection of the same kind, not a different connector. Step 3Check the result tdk collection get --proj finance --name sales_source A request that changes nothing is rejected: The collection update request has nothing to update. When a rename and a connection change are passed together, the rename is applied first.

The collection's type, and therefore its group, are immutable. There is no command that moves a collection to another group, and CollectionUpdate carries no field for it. Changing connectors means deleting the collection and creating it again. --storage-path applies to new artifacts only. Existing data versions keep the path stamped at write time. See tdk collection update for the full option list.

Before you begin Register a Function Step 1Delete the function tdk fn delete --coll reporting --name summarize --confirm delete --confirm takes the literal word delete. Omit it and tdk prompts for it instead. Step 2Confirm it is gone tdk fn list --coll reporting

Deleting a function does not delete the tables it wrote. Other functions that depend on those tables are frozen — they stay registered and stop running until re-registered against tables that still exist — rather than deleted along with the function that produced them. See tdk fn delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Collection A function is a Python file and the function inside it, registered into a collection. The kind of function a collection accepts follows from the group it was created in: a source collection takes publishers, a destination collection takes subscribers, and a data product collection takes transformers. Step 1Register the function tdk fn register \ --coll reporting \ --path summarize.py::summarize \ --description "Rolls orders up by region" --path names the file and the function inside it as file.py::function_name. Re-register after every code change — tdk fn register creates a new function version each time. Step 2Confirm it exists tdk fn get --coll reporting --name summarize --show-history on tdk fn get lists every version the function has gone through, newest first.

tdk fn register rejects a name that already exists in the collection unless you pass --update, which registers the new code as the next version of the same function instead of erroring. tdk fn register \ --coll reporting \ --path summarize.py::summarize \ --update
--reuse-tables tells the registration to keep any of the function's output tables that already exist in the collection, rather than erroring because they are already there.

A function registers enabled by default. --enabled false at registration time, or tdk fn disable --coll <collection> --name <function> afterward, stops it from running without deleting it. tdk fn enable turns it back on.
Trigger the function or wait for whatever trigger it was given to fire it on its own. See tdk fn register for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project A group sits inside a project and holds collections. Which group a collection is created in fixes what that collection can hold, and that choice is permanent. Three groups exist in every project already: sources for publishers, destinations for subscribers, and default for transformers. A group you create yourself holds transformers too, so the reason to add one is organising a pipeline rather than unlocking anything new. Step 1Create the group tdk group create \ --proj finance \ --name bronze \ --description "Raw ingested data" --proj names the project the group belongs to, and can be omitted when a project is pinned. Collections created in bronze hold transformers, the same as default. Step 2Confirm it exists tdk group list --proj finance The three seeded groups are listed alongside it. System groups cannot be renamed or deleted.

Collections in a user-created group hold transformers, which default already does, so grouping is organisational. The medallion layout, bronze then silver then gold, is a common convention for naming the stages of a pipeline; it is a docs convention rather than something Tabsdata enforces.
documents.s: Why add a group at all

documents.t: Create a Collection in the group. See tdk group create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Group Deleting a group deletes the collections inside it. Like the other deletes, it takes a typed confirmation. Step 1Check what the group holds tdk collection list --proj finance --group bronze Every collection listed here goes with the group. Step 2Delete it tdk group delete \ --proj finance \ --name bronze --confirm takes the literal string delete. The three system groups cannot be deleted, so this only ever applies to a group you created.

The group's collections are deleted with it, along with their tables and functions. Functions in other collections that depended on those tables are frozen rather than deleted: they stay registered and stop running until they are re-registered against tables that exist. See tdk group delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Group tdk group update changes a group's name or description. The collections inside it are untouched, and so is what those collections are allowed to hold. Step 1Rename the group, or change its description tdk group update \ --proj finance \ --name bronze \ --new-name raw \ --description "Raw ingested data" --name is the current name and --new-name the replacement. Either --new-name or --description is enough on its own. Step 2Check the result tdk group get --proj finance --name raw The three system groups, default, sources and destinations, cannot be updated at all.

A collection's type follows from the group it was created in, and renaming the group does not revisit that. A collection created in sources still holds publishers after the group is called something else. See tdk group update for the full option list.
documents.s: What a rename does not change

documents.t: Before you begin Install Tabsdata Start a Server A project is the outermost resource within Tabsdata server and allows full isolation from workflows and resources in other projects. Step 1Create the project tdk project create \ --name finance \ --description "Subscription billing" --name starts with a letter and continues with letters, digits or underscores, up to 100 characters, and has to be unique on the server. --description is optional and capped at 200 characters. Step 2Confirm it exists and see its groups tdk project list tdk group list --proj finance The three seeded groups appear straight away. A collection created in sources holds publishers, one in destinations holds subscribers, and one in default or any group you add yourself holds transformers.

Most commands take --proj to say which project they act on. Pinning one makes it the default: tdk project pin --name finance Every later command then acts on finance unless it passes --proj explicitly.
documents.s: Pin it, so later commands need no --proj

documents.t: A project on its own holds nothing. Create a collection in one of its groups: Create a Collection. See tdk project create for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project warning Deleting a project deletes all resources nested inside of it, including function code, execution logs, and table data. This action cannot be reversed. Step 1Check what the project holds tdk group list --proj finance tdk collection list --proj finance Step 2Delete it tdk project delete \ --name finance --confirm takes the literal string delete. Anything else, including y or yes, cancels the command and leaves the project standing.

Every group and collection in the project is deleted with it, along with the tables those collections held and the functions registered in them. The project's name is freed and can be reused immediately. See tdk project delete for the full option list.

Before you begin Create a Project tdk project update changes a project's name or its description. Both are metadata: renaming a project does not move, rebuild or re-path anything inside it. Step 1Rename the project, or change its description tdk project update \ --name finance \ --new-name billing \ --description "Subscription billing and dunning" --name names the project as it stands now; --new-name is what it becomes. Passing only --description changes the description and leaves the name alone. Step 2Check the result tdk project get --name billing A request that changes nothing is rejected rather than silently accepted, with The project update request has nothing to update.

The project keeps its id, its groups, its collections and their data. Anything referring to the project by id keeps working; anything referring to it by name, a pinned project or a script passing --proj, needs the new name. See tdk project update for the full option list.
documents.s: What a rename does not change

documents.t: This is the pipeline you build in the Getting Started tutorial. Click any node to inspect its Python code or table schema. Tabsdata · Tutorial Pipeline · Execution View Publisher pub pub Publisher Committed Table persons persons //tutorial ✓Data Available Transformer tfr tfr Transformer Committed Table spanish spanish //tutorial ✓Data Available Table french french //tutorial ✓Data Available Table german german //tutorial ✓Data Available Click any node to inspect code or schema

The pipeline has three stages: Publisher (pub) — reads CSV files from disk, renames columns, and writes to the persons table. Transformer (tfr) — reads persons, filters rows by language, and writes three output tables. Tables — spanish, french, and german each hold the filtered rows for subscribers to consume. The dashed blue line between persons → tfr represents a data-dependency edge: the transformer triggers automatically whenever persons is updated.
A publisher is a Tabsdata function that reads data from an external source, such as file system or database, and writes the data to one or more tables in the Tabsdata server.

POub Every publisher setup has the same three assets: a connection template that knows how to reach the external system, a collection that owns the connection, and a publisher function registered into the collection. Explore them below (click any asset, or its ? for context), then trigger the publisher to see versioned tables land: Tabsdata server collection · world? ▶ Trigger publisher Database PostgreSQL ? PostgreSQL · external Reachable Connection conn-postgres.yaml ? Publisher read_world ? Table country ? //world No versions yet Table city ? //world No versions yet Here is an example publisher named read_sales. It reads three sales csv files, checks if their last modified date is after 1st Jan 2021, and writes them to the Tabsdata tables of the same name. This publisher executes automatically as soon as a new commit occurs on the new_customer table: import tabsdata as td @td.publisher( source=td.LocalFileSource( [ "/users/username/opt/sales-staging/us/us_sales.csv", "/users/username/opt/sales-staging/eu/eu_sales.csv", "/users/username/opt/sales-staging/emea/emea_sales.csv", ], initial_last_modified="2021-01-01", ), tables=["us_sales", "eu_sales", "emea_sales"], trigger_by="new_customer", ) def read_sales(tf1: td.TableFrame, tf2: td.TableFrame, tf3: td.TableFrame): return tf1, tf2, tf3 When you define a publisher, you specify the name of the publisher, the data to read, and the names of the Tabsdata tables to write to. If you want the publisher to execute automatically, you need to specify the Tabsdata tables that will trigger the publisher when a commit occurs for one of those tables in the trigger_by parameter. To create and run a Tabsdata publisher, complete the following tasks: Define a publisher - Define a publisher to configure the parameters that govern the reading of data into the Tabsdata server. The syntax for defining a publisher differs depending on the system that the publisher reads from. For details, see the supported source connectors below. Register the publisher - Register the publisher with a Tabsdata collection. A publisher can only write output tables to the collection that it is registered with. For information about registering functions, see here. Execute the publisher - Execute the publisher by initiating a trigger. Once executed, the publisher takes the input data, processes it as defined in the function logic, and writes the output tables in the Tabsdata server. By default, publishers do not have any triggers. For more information about executing a function, see here. Below is the list of sources connectors that are currently supported natively in Tabsdata. Beyond these, you can connect with other external systems as per your need using connector plugins. Local File System Amazon S3 Azure Blob Storage Databricks Db2 Db2 CDC Google Cloud Storage Kafka MariaDB Microsoft SQL Server MySQL CDC MySQL Oracle Postgres PostgreSQL CDC Salesforce SOQL Query Salesforce Reports Grok for Log Files

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project This tutorial shows how to set up an Amazon S3 publisher that reads one or more files out of an S3 bucket and writes them into one or more Tabsdata Tables What you’ll do Configure a connection to S3 Write and Register a Publisher Function Trigger the publisher function

A Connection is a resource that stores the configuration and credentials needed to access an external system. Publishers use the credentials stored in a connection to authenticate with AWS. Step 1Generate a connection template tdk connection template --type s3-file-in --file conn-s3.yaml This creates a connection document within your working directory under the file name specified in the --file cli command. Step 2Fill in the bucket, the region, and the credentials within the connection document tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3SrcConn spec: bucket: 'acme-ingest' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' secret_access_key: 'secret:wJalrXUtnFEMI0EXAMPLEKEY' bucket:strrequired region:strrequired credentials:AwsAccessSecretKeyrequired base_path:stroptional Fill in the bucket name, region, access_key_id, secret_access_key, and base path. Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in connection document (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-s3.yaml

the filled-in connection document must be attached to a collection that contains (or will contain) the function using the connection credentials. Step 4Bind connection to a new or existing collection Create a New Collection Attach to an Existing Collection tdk collection create --name hr_files --group sources --conn-file conn-s3.yaml tdk collection update --name hr_files --conn-file conn-s3.yaml
documents.s: Bind connection document to a collection

documents.t: Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_files.py 1from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src 3 4 5@publisher( 6 source=S3Src( 1 paths=["departments.csv", "employees.csv"], 8 ), 2 output_tables=["departments", "employees"], 10) 3def read_files(departments, employees): 4 return (departments[0], employees[0]) 1paths S3 paths to read. Each element positionally maps to a function argument on line 11. 2output_tables Tabsdata tables function output is written to. Each name maps positionally to data returned on line 12. 3function arguments Data ingested from S3, positionally mapped and represented as Python function arguments. 4return Data the function outputs, mapped positionally to output tables defined on line 9. Each entry in the paths parameter represents the data contained in the file or files at that S3 path. Each paths entry maps positionally to an argument in the function body. Because Tabsdata supports wildcard expansion, a path can match either a single file, represented as a single-element list of TableFrames, or multiple files, represented as a list containing one TableFrame for each matched file. Variables listed in the function body's return statement represent output data and map positionally to the Tabsdata tables declared in the output_tables parameter. Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll hr_files --path read_files.py::read_files
documents.s: Write and Register a Publisher Function

documents.t: Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_files.py 1from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.azureblob import AzureBlobSrc 3from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat 4 5 6@publisher( 7 source=AzureBlobSrc( 1 paths=["departments.csv", "employees_*.csv"], 9 ), 2 output_tables=["departments", "employees"], 11) 3def read_files(departments, employees): 4 return (departments[0], concat(employees)) 1paths Blob paths to read. Each element positionally maps to a function argument on line 12. 2output_tables Tabsdata tables function output is written to. Each name maps positionally to data returned on line 13. 3function arguments Data ingested from Azure Blob Storage, positionally mapped and represented as Python function arguments. A path with no glob arrives as a single-element list; departments.csv matches exactly one file, so departments[0] is that file. A glob can match several, so employees is concat()-ed into one table. 4return Data the function outputs, mapped positionally to output tables defined on line 10. Each entry in the paths parameter represents the data contained in the file or files at that blob path. Each paths entry maps positionally to an argument in the function body. Because Tabsdata supports wildcard expansion, a path can match either a single file, represented as a single-element list of TableFrames, or multiple files, represented as a list containing one TableFrame for each matched file. Since each output table takes exactly one TableFrame, a publisher combines a multi-file match with concat() before returning it; a single-file match just needs [0] to unwrap the list. Variables listed in the function body's return statement represent output data and map positionally to the Tabsdata tables declared in the output_tables parameter. Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll hr_files --path read_files.py::read_files

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The Db2 CDC publisher captures row-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) from a Db2 database using SQL Replication. Db2 SQL Replication captures changes into shadow CD (Change Data) tables that the ASN capture program (asncap) populates in the background, so tables names the CD tables rather than the original source tables — the connector resolves the source table from ASN.IBMSNAP_REGISTER automatically. A long-lived stream worker hands a flushed batch to the publisher on each rollover, so this uses @stream_publisher rather than @publisher. What you’ll do Configure a connection to Db2 Write and Register the Stream Publisher

Step 1Generate a connection template tdk connection template --type db2-cdc --file conn-db2-cdc.yaml Step 2Fill in the URI and credentials, and bind it to a collection tdk collection create --name sales_cdc --group sources --conn-file conn-db2-cdc.yaml

Step 3Build the stream publisher file locally read_sales_changes.py 1from tabsdatak.api import stream_publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2CdcStreamSrc 3 4 5@stream_publisher( 6 source=Db2CdcStreamSrc( 1 tables=["ASN.TD_T__ORDERS", "ASN.TD_T__CUSTOMERS"], 2 start_from="tail", 9 ), 3 flush_interval_mins=2, 4 output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], 12) 5def read_sales_changes(orders, customers): 6 return (orders[0], customers[0]) 1tables Qualified cd_schema.cd_table names of the CD tables to track, not the source tables. 2start_from "tail" begins at each table's current watermark and never backfills. 3flush_interval_mins Fallback rollover window in whole minutes if the capture table's own threshold has not fired. 4output_tables One output table per tracked CD table, in the same order. 5function arguments One TableFramesSpec parameter per source slot, always array mode. No ctx parameter. 6return One frame per output table, the same order as output_tables. start_from also accepts "head" to replay each tracked CD table from the origin, or an explicit CommitSeqPosition(seq=...), TableCommitSeqPosition(seqs={...}), or TimestampPosition(ts=...). A stream publisher takes no trigger_by and must not declare a ctx parameter — it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction. Step 4Register the stream publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll sales_cdc --path read_sales_changes.py::read_sales_changes

documents.t: Rollover fires on whichever comes first: flush_interval_mins, or a threshold set via src_cfg, a config mapping over allowed CDC keys: src_cfg key Default Description tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows 10,000 Flush to the working directory when row count in memory reaches this limit. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes None Flush when byte size in memory reaches this limit. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs 60 Flush when this many seconds have elapsed since the last flush. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_rows None Stage when total rows on disk reach this limit. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_bytes None Stage when total bytes on disk reach this limit. tabsdata.cdc.trigger.max_secs 60 Stage when this many seconds have elapsed since the last stage. tabsdata.cdc.poll_interval_seconds — Seconds between polling the CD tables for new changes. db2.cdc.blocking_timeout_seconds — Timeout in seconds for blocking reads. db2.cdc.fetch_size — Server-side fetch size for reading CD table rows. db2.cdc.logging_level — Log level for the capture reader. source=Db2CdcStreamSrc( tables=["ASN.TD_T__ORDERS"], start_from="tail", src_cfg={"tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows": 5000}, )
columns_format (default "columns", or "struct" / "map") and flatten_columns (default True) control how the new — and, where present, old — column values lay out on each emitted change row.

TRUNCATE TABLE operations are not captured. All CD tables must exist before the stream publisher is registered; the connector does not perform runtime table discovery. Schema changes on tracked tables are supported, but performing one on a table with CDC enabled is a complex administration effort on the Db2 side. Stop the stream publisher while schema changes are being made.
Refer to the IBM Db2 documentation for comprehensive and up-to-date configuration instructions.

SQL Replication requires archive logging so the capture agent can read the recovery log. mkdir $HOME/archive mkdir $HOME/backup db2 UPDATE DB CFG FOR sales USING logarchmeth1 disk:$HOME/archive/ db2 BACKUP DB sales TO $HOME/backup/ A full backup is required after enabling archive logging.

The ASN control tables store capture metadata. Create them using the asnclp tool: asnclp << EOF SET SERVER CAPTURE TO DB sales; SET CAPTURE SCHEMA SOURCE ASN; CREATE CONTROL TABLES FOR CAPTURE SERVER; EOF
asncap capture_server=sales capture_schema=ASN & The capture agent must be running before the connector can capture changes.

asnclp << EOF SET SERVER CAPTURE TO DB sales; SET CAPTURE SCHEMA SOURCE ASN; SET RUN SCRIPT NOW STOP ON SQL ERROR ON; CREATE REGISTRATION ( sales_schema.orders ) DIFFERENTIAL REFRESH IMAGE BOTH PREFIX _ CAPTURE ALL; EOF Option Description DIFFERENTIAL REFRESH Only changed rows are captured, not full table snapshots. IMAGE BOTH Both before-image and after-image are recorded for updates. PREFIX _ Before-image column names are prefixed with underscore. CAPTURE ALL All column changes are captured.

documents.t: Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_files.py 1from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.gcs import GCSSrc 3from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat 4 5 6@publisher( 7 source=GCSSrc( 1 paths=["departments.csv", "employees_*.csv"], 9 initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00Z", 10 ), 2 output_tables=["departments", "employees"], 12) 3def read_files(departments, employees): 4 return (departments[0], concat(employees)) 1paths GCS paths to read. Each element positionally maps to a function argument on line 13. 2output_tables Tabsdata tables function output is written to. Each name maps positionally to data returned on line 14. 3function arguments Data ingested from Google Cloud Storage, positionally mapped and represented as Python function arguments. A path with no glob arrives as a single-element list; departments.csv matches exactly one file, so departments[0] is that file. A glob can match several, so employees is concat()-ed into one table. 4return Data the function outputs, mapped positionally to output tables defined on line 11. Each entry in the paths parameter represents the data contained in the file or files at that GCS path. Each paths entry maps positionally to an argument in the function body. Because Tabsdata supports wildcard expansion, a path can match either a single file, represented as a single-element list of TableFrames, or multiple files, represented as a list containing one TableFrame for each matched file. Since each output table takes exactly one TableFrame, a publisher combines a multi-file match with concat() before returning it; a single-file match just needs [0] to unwrap the list. Variables listed in the function body's return statement represent output data and map positionally to the Tabsdata tables declared in the output_tables parameter. Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The grok function is a powerful log parsing tool for TableFrames that extracts structured data from log files and similar text formats. Originally developed for log analysis, it transforms a single text column into multiple typed columns by applying grok patterns with named captures. Grok is based on the Elasticsearch implementation and follows the same pattern syntax. For comprehensive pattern documentation, see the official Elasticsearch Grok documentation and the predefined pattern library. Grok uses regular expressions with predefined patterns to parse text. Each pattern includes named captures that become columns in your result. The function takes three inputs: Column Expression: Any expression that selects one column containing text to parse Pattern: A grok pattern string with named captures Schema: A mapping that defines output column names and data types for each capture While not technically a full-fledged connector like S3, Postgres, or Databricks, the grok log parser can be used with Publishers for Local File Systems and Object Storage in order to parse and convert single column logs into structured, tabular data. What you’ll do Configure a connection to the log source Write and Register a Publisher Function Trigger the publisher function
documents.s: Publish data from log files with Grok

documents.t: Log files sit on disk or in object storage, so the connection is a file connection rather than anything grok-specific. A local directory: Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type local-file-in --file conn-logs.yaml Step 2Point base_path at the log directory conn-logs.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.localfile:LocalFileSrcConn spec: base_path: '/var/log/acme' Reading logs out of a bucket instead means s3-file-in or az-file-in here. Nothing else on this page changes: the parsing happens in the publisher body, not in the connection.

documents.t: Grok patterns use the format %{name:alias:extract:definition} where: name: A predefined pattern name (e.g., IPV4, WORD, INT) alias: A custom name for this capture (becomes the capture name) extract: Reserved for future use (not used in current version) definition: A regular expression definition (required if name is not specified) The publisher function ingests the log file as a single-column tableframe and applies the grok method which accepts the column to parse, the string pattern that defines the structure data in the column, and a schema that defines how the parsed text should be structured in the output Tableframe. read_access_logs.py 1from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.localfile import LocalFileSrc, SrcFileFormat 3from tabsdatak.tableframe.grok import ColumnDefinition 4from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes import String, Int32, Int64 5 6PATTERN = ( 7 r"%{IPV4:client_ip} " 8 r"%{USER:ident} " 9 r"%{USER:auth} " 10 r"\[%{HTTPDATE:timestamp}\] " 11 r'"%{WORD:method} ' 12 r'%{URIPATHPARAM:request} ' 13 r'HTTP/%{NUMBER:http_version}" ' 14 r"%{INT:response_code} %{INT:bytes}" 15) 16 17SCHEMA = { 18 "client_ip": ColumnDefinition("ip_address", String), 19 "method": ColumnDefinition("http_method", String), 20 "response_code": ColumnDefinition("status_code", Int32), 21 "bytes": ColumnDefinition("response_bytes", Int64), 22 "timestamp": ColumnDefinition("request_time", String), 23} 24 25 26@publisher( 27 source=LocalFileSrc( 1 paths=["access.log"], 29 format=SrcFileFormat.CSV, 30 format_cfg={ 31 SrcFileFormat.CSV: {"has_header": False, "separator": "\\x00"}, 32 }, 33 ), 2 output_tables=["access_logs"], 35) 3def read_access_logs(lines): 37 if lines is None: 38 return (None,) 4 return (lines[0].grok("column_1", PATTERN, SCHEMA),) 1paths Local file path to read. Its single element maps to the function argument on line 36. 2output_tables Tabsdata table the parsed rows are written to, matching the value returned on line 39. 3function arguments Raw log lines read from the file, represented as a Python function argument. 4return Grok parses the text column into typed columns using PATTERN and SCHEMA, and the result is returned as the output table. lines column_1 203.0.113.10 - - [10/Oct/2026:13:55:01 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 512 1 row access_logs ip_addressstr http_methodstr status_codei32 response_bytesi64 request_timestr 203.0.113.10 GET 200 512 10/Oct/2026:13:55:01 +0000 1 row Step 4Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll log_src --path read_access_logs.py::read_access_logs

Step 5Build the stream publisher file locally read_flight_events.py 1from tabsdatak.api import stream_publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.kafka import KafkaStreamSrc 3 4FLIGHT_EVENT_SCHEMA = open("flight_event.schema.json").read() 5 6 7@stream_publisher( 8 source=KafkaStreamSrc( 1 topic="flight_events", 2 data_format="json", 3 schema=FLIGHT_EVENT_SCHEMA, 12 ), 4 flush_interval_mins=2, 5 output_tables=["flight_events"], 15) 6def read_flight_events(events): 7 return events[0] 1topic Kafka topic to consume; also the emitted table name. 2data_format Payload wire format: "avro", "json", or a Protobuf(message_name=...) marker. 3schema Schema definition string for data_format, required even in schema-registry mode. 4flush_interval_mins Fallback rollover window in whole minutes if the topic's own threshold has not fired. 5output_tables A Kafka source always has exactly one output table. 6function arguments One TableFramesSpec parameter for the single source slot, always array mode. No ctx parameter. 7return One frame for the topic's output table. The source parameter defines the Kafka topic to consume from, the format of the messages, and the schema used to parse them. dlq_topic on KafkaStreamSrc names an optional topic that messages failing deserialization are produced to, instead of failing the stream.

A stream publisher can be stopped and started without deleting it, which is useful for maintenance on the Kafka side or to hold off consuming while other setup finishes: tdk fn stop --coll events --name read_flight_events tdk fn start --coll events --name read_flight_events Registering with --disabled puts the publisher in the collection without starting consumption; start it later with the command above once you're ready.

See Installing Third-Party Database Drivers for how to declare it during installation. The MySQL CDC publisher captures row-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) from a MySQL database by reading its binary log (binlog) in real time. A long-lived stream worker follows the binlog and hands a flushed batch to the publisher on each rollover, so this uses @stream_publisher rather than @publisher. What you’ll do Configure a connection to MySQL Write and Register the Stream Publisher

Step 1Generate a connection template tdk connection template --type mysql-cdc --file conn-mysql-cdc.yaml Step 2Fill in the URI and credentials, and bind it to a collection tdk collection create --name sales_cdc --group sources --conn-file conn-mysql-cdc.yaml The connection holds the URI and credentials for MySQLCdcStreamSrcConn, which is separate from the batch MySQLSrcConn connector: it also reserves a server_id, the replica identifier the binlog stream uses. Each concurrent CDC connection against the same MySQL server needs a distinct server_id.

Step 3Build the stream publisher file locally read_sales_changes.py 1from tabsdatak.api import stream_publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLCdcStreamSrc 3 4 5@stream_publisher( 6 source=MySQLCdcStreamSrc( 1 tables=["sales.orders", "sales.customers"], 2 start_from="tail", 9 ), 3 flush_interval_mins=2, 4 output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], 12) 5def read_sales_changes(orders, customers): 6 return (orders[0], customers[0]) 1tables Qualified schema.table names to track. 2start_from "tail" begins at the current binlog position and never backfills. 3flush_interval_mins Fallback rollover window in whole minutes if the binlog's own threshold has not fired. 4output_tables One output table per tracked table, in the same order. 5function arguments One TableFramesSpec parameter per source slot, always array mode. No ctx parameter. 6return One frame per output table, the same order as output_tables. start_from also accepts "head" to begin at the oldest retained binlog, or an explicit GtidPosition(gtid=...), BinlogPosition(file=..., pos=...), or TimestampPosition(ts=...). A stream publisher takes no trigger_by and must not declare a ctx parameter — it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction. Step 4Register the stream publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll sales_cdc --path read_sales_changes.py::read_sales_changes

TRUNCATE TABLE operations are not captured. All tables must exist in the source database before the stream publisher is registered. Tables created afterward are not captured. Schema changes on tracked tables (ALTER TABLE, ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN) are picked up automatically.
Refer to the MySQL documentation for comprehensive and up-to-date configuration instructions.

Add the following to your MySQL configuration file (my.cnf or my.ini) and restart the server: [mysqld] server-id = 1 log_bin = mysql-bin binlog_format = ROW binlog_row_image = FULL gtid_mode = ON enforce_gtid_consistency = ON Parameter Description server-id Enables binary logging with a unique server identifier. binlog_format = ROW Row-based format captures individual column values rather than SQL statements. binlog_row_image = FULL Logs all columns for every change, not just modified ones. gtid_mode = ON Required for resuming from a precise position across server restarts.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project note The PostgreSQL CDC connector needs a database driver that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. See Installing Third-Party Database Drivers for how to declare it during installation. The PostgreSQL CDC publisher captures row-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) from a PostgreSQL database using WAL logical replication, decoded by the wal2json output plugin. Postgres logical replication requires a replication slot — a persistent cursor on the WAL the database will not garbage-collect until the consumer confirms. A long-lived stream worker hands a flushed batch to the publisher on each rollover, so this uses @stream_publisher rather than @publisher. What you’ll do Configure a connection to Postgres Write and Register the Stream Publisher

Step 1Generate a connection template tdk connection template --type postgres-cdc --file conn-postgres-cdc.yaml Step 2Fill in the URI and credentials, and bind it to a collection tdk collection create --name sales_cdc --group sources --conn-file conn-postgres-cdc.yaml PostgresCdcStreamSrcConn mirrors the batch PostgresSrcConn for the URI and credentials, but the connecting role must carry the REPLICATION attribute. The replication slot and publication live on the publisher's source object instead of the connection, so one connection can front several sources as long as each uses a distinct slot.

Step 3Build the stream publisher file locally read_sales_changes.py 1from tabsdatak.api import stream_publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresCdcStreamSrc 3 4 5@stream_publisher( 6 source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc( 1 tables=["sales.orders", "sales.customers"], 2 replication_slot="sales_cdc_slot", 3 replication_slot_behavior="create", 4 start_from="tail", 11 ), 5 flush_interval_mins=2, 6 output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], 14) 7def read_sales_changes(orders, customers): 8 return (orders[0], customers[0]) 1tables Qualified schema.table names to track. 2replication_slot Logical replication slot this source attaches to. 3replication_slot_behavior "create" makes the slot if missing; "reuse" (default) requires it to already exist. 4start_from "tail" begins at the current WAL position and never backfills. 5flush_interval_mins Fallback rollover window in whole minutes if the WAL's own threshold has not fired. 6output_tables One output table per tracked table, in the same order. 7function arguments One TableFramesSpec parameter per source slot, always array mode. No ctx parameter. 8return One frame per output table, the same order as output_tables. start_from also accepts "head" to replay from the oldest retained WAL, or an explicit LsnPosition(lsn=...). A stream publisher takes no trigger_by and must not declare a ctx parameter — it runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction. Step 4Register the stream publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll sales_cdc --path read_sales_changes.py::read_sales_changes

columns_format (default "columns", or "struct" / "map") and flatten_columns (default True) control how the new — and, where present, old — column values lay out on each emitted change row.

TRUNCATE TABLE operations are not captured. All tables must exist in the source database before the stream publisher is registered. Schema changes on tracked tables (ALTER TABLE, ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN) are picked up automatically. Abandoned replication slots cause unbounded WAL growth. Monitor slot lag via pg_replication_slots and drop unused slots promptly.
Refer to the PostgreSQL documentation for comprehensive and up-to-date configuration instructions.
Add the following to postgresql.conf and restart the server: wal_level = logical max_replication_slots = 4 # at least 1 per CDC consumer max_wal_senders = 4 # at least 1 per CDC consumer

The wal2json extension must be installed on the PostgreSQL server. On Debian/Ubuntu, it is available as a system package: # Adjust version number to match your PostgreSQL version apt-get install postgresql-17-wal2json For installation instructions and detailed documentation, see the wal2json project.

Every Salesforce object carries a SystemModStamp column, and Tabsdata reads it to publish only the rows that changed since the previous run. Two things have to be true for that to work: SystemModStamp appears in the SELECT list, and the WHERE clause compares it against the $lastModified placeholder. On the first run $lastModified takes the value of initial_last_modified. On every later run it takes the highest SystemModStamp seen so far, so each trigger reads forward from where the last one stopped. Deletions are invisible to that comparison, because a deleted row stops appearing rather than getting a newer timestamp. Set include_deleted to True to read deleted records too, which is what makes an incremental load able to tell that a row went away.

Parameter Required What it does queries yes SOQL queries, one per output table, in order initial_last_modified no Starting timestamp for the first incremental run include_deleted no Reads deleted records as well. Defaults to False instance_url no Disambiguates the org when the credentials map to several version no Salesforce API version. Defaults to the latest

A query that returns no rows fills its slot with None rather than an empty frame. Returning None for a table tells Tabsdata to keep the previous version as current instead of committing a new one, which is the usual outcome of an incremental run with nothing new to read: read_when_available.py @publisher( source=SalesforceSrc( queries=["SELECT Id, Email, SystemModStamp FROM Contact " "WHERE SystemModStamp > $lastModified"], initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000+0000", ), output_tables=["contacts"], ) def read_when_available(contacts): if contacts is None: return (None,) return (contacts[0],)

Authentication fails. Check that the username is the Salesforce username and not the email address, and that the security token matches the current password. Resetting either one invalidates the token. Every run re-reads everything. The query is missing $lastModified in its WHERE clause, or SystemModStamp is missing from the SELECT list. Both are required for the incremental read. Rows disappear from the source but stay in the table. include_deleted defaults to False, so deletions are not read at all. Wrong org. One set of credentials that maps to several orgs needs instance_url on the connection to pick between them.

Step 4Bind connection to a new or existing collection Create a New Collection Attach to an Existing Collection tdk collection create --name sf_reports --group sources --conn-file conn-sf-report.yaml tdk collection update --name sf_reports --conn-file conn-sf-report.yaml

documents.t: Step 5Build the publisher file locally read_contacts.py 1from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceReportSrc 3 4 5@publisher( 6 source=SalesforceReportSrc( 1 reports=["contacts"], 8 column_name_strategy="columnName", 9 filter=[ 10 ("COUNTRY", "equals", "USA"), 11 ("COUNTRY", "equals", "France"), 12 ], 13 filter_logic="1 or 2", 14 last_modified_column="LAST_MODIFIED_DATE", 15 initial_last_modified="2026-01-01T00:00:00.000+0000", 16 ), 2 output_tables=["contacts"], 18) 3def read_contacts(contacts): 4 return (contacts[0],) 1reports Salesforce report to read. Its single element maps to the function argument on line 19. 2output_tables Tabsdata table the report rows are written to, matching the value returned on line 20. 3function arguments Report rows read from Salesforce, represented as a Python function argument. 4return Data the function outputs, mapped to the output table defined on line 17. Each entry in the reports list parameter represents the data within that report. Each reports entry maps positionally to an argument in the function body. Variables listed in the function body's return statement represent output data and map positionally to the Tabsdata tables declared in the output_tables parameter. Step 6Register the publisher into the collection tdk fn register --coll sf_reports --path read_contacts.py::read_contacts

Object Type FIRST_NAME str LAST_NAME str EMAIL str COUNTRY str
Table schema defines the structure of a table by listing its columns and their data types. Object Type FIRST_NAME str LAST_NAME str EMAIL str COUNTRY str

reports takes one report or a list of them, referenced by id or by name. Which of the two is meant is inferred from the value, and find_report_by states it outright when the inference would guess wrong. A report referenced by name uses what Salesforce calls the report unique name, also shown as the developer name, rather than the label displayed in the UI. column_name_strategy decides where the output column names come from. A Salesforce report carries both a columnName and a label for every column: CREATED_ALIAS against alias, for instance. The choice sets the column names in the resulting Tabsdata table, and it also sets the names the filters have to use, so a filter written against labels breaks when the strategy is columnName.
documents.s: Naming a report, and naming its columns

documents.t: Each filter is a tuple of a column, an operator, and a value, in the form Salesforce report queries already use. More than one filter goes in a list. filter_logic states how those filters combine, referring to them by position: the first filter in the list is 1, the second is 2, and so on. "1 or 2" accepts a row matching either, and "1 or (2 and 3)" groups them. Without filter_logic, the filters carry no stated relationship between them.

initial_last_modified sets where the first run starts, as a string in Salesforce datetime format with the timezone included. last_modified_column names the column the comparison runs against, and that column has to be in the report for the read to work. It defaults to None, which reads the whole report on every run.

Parameter Required What it does reports yes One report or a list, by id or by name column_name_strategy no columnName (default) or label, setting output column names find_report_by no id or name, when the reference is ambiguous filter no Tuples of column, operator, value filter_logic no How the filters combine, by position initial_last_modified no Starting timestamp for the first incremental run last_modified_column no Report column driving the incremental read

A filter matches nothing. Filters use whichever names column_name_strategy selected, so a filter written against alias fails under columnName and needs CREATED_ALIAS instead. The report is not found by name. Salesforce matches the report unique name, not the label in the UI. Set find_report_by to name and pass the unique name, or reference the report by id. Every run re-reads the whole report. last_modified_column is unset, or the column it names is missing from the report definition.

A subscriber is a Tabsdata function that reads from tables in the Tabsdata server and writes them to external destinations such as file systems or databases. For example, you can create a subscriber to write the Tabsdata tables that it is subscribed to and write them to an AWS S3 instance.

A subscriber setup mirrors a publisher's, with the flow reversed: existing Tabsdata tables feed a subscriber function, which writes them out through a connection owned by a destination collection. Explore the pieces below (click any asset, or its ? for context), then trigger the subscriber to sync data out: Tabsdata server collection · warehouse? ▶ Trigger subscriber Table vendors ? //sales Committed Table items ? //sales Committed Connection conn-mysql-dest.yaml ? Subscriber write_sales ? Database MySQL ? MySQL · external Not yet synced When you define a subscriber, you specify the name of the subscriber, the Tabsdata tables to write, and destination properties to write to. By default a subscriber is triggered by a new commit to any of its input tables. To create and run a Tabsdata subscriber, complete the following tasks: Define a subscriber - Define a subscriber to configure the parameters that govern the writing of data from the Tabsdata server. The syntax for defining a subscriber differs depending on the system that the subscriber writes to. For details, see the supported destination connectors below. Register the subscriber - Register the subscriber with a Tabsdata collection. A subscriber can read from tables outside the collection it is registered with. For information about registering functions, see here. Execute the subscriber - Execute the subscriber by initiating its trigger. Once executed, the subscriber reads the Tabsdata tables, and writes the output data to the external systems. By default, subscribers are triggered when any of the input tables receive a new commit. However, you can define any Tabsdata table to act as a trigger for a subscriber. For more information, see here. Below is the list of destination connectors that are currently supported natively in Tabsdata. Beyond these, you can connect with other external systems as per your need using connector plugins. Local File System Amazon S3 AWS Glue - Iceberg tables Azure Blob Storage Big Query ClickHouse Databricks Apache Druid Google Cloud Storage MariaDB MongoDB Microsoft SQL Server MySQL Oracle Postgres Snowflake StarRocks

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project This tutorial shows how to set up an Amazon S3 subscriber that writes one or more Tabsdata Tables to an S3 bucket What you’ll do Configure a connection to S3 Write and Register a Subscriber Function Trigger the subscriber function

A Connection is a resource that stores the configuration and credentials needed to access an external system. Subscribers use the credentials stored in a connection to authenticate with AWS. Step 1Generate a connection template tdk connection template --type s3-file-out --file conn-s3.yaml This creates a connection document within your working directory under the file name specified in the --file cli command. Step 2Fill in the bucket, the region, and the credentials within the connection document tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3DestConn spec: bucket: 'acme-exports' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' secret_access_key: 'secret:wJalrXUtnFEMI0EXAMPLEKEY' bucket:strrequired region:strrequired credentials:AwsAccessSecretKeyrequired base_path:stroptional Fill in the bucket name, region, access_key_id, secret_access_key, and base path. Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in connection document (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-s3.yaml

The filled-in connection document must be attached to a collection that contains (or will contain) the function using the connection credentials. Step 4Bind connection to a new or existing collection Create a New Collection Attach to an Existing Collection tdk collection create --name exports --group destinations --conn-file conn-s3.yaml tdk collection update --name exports --conn-file conn-s3.yaml

documents.t: Step 5Build the subscriber file locally write_files.py 1from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec 2from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Dest 3 4 5@subscriber( 6 destination=S3Dest( 1 paths=["departments_${EXEC_PLAN_TS}.parquet", "employees_${EXEC_PLAN_TS}.parquet"], 8 ), 2 input_tables=["hr/departments", "hr/employees"], 10) 3def write_files(departments, employees): 4 return (departments, employees) 1paths S3 paths to write to. Each element positionally maps to a function argument on line 11. 2input_tables Tabsdata tables function input is read from. Each name maps positionally to a function argument on line 11. 3function arguments Data read from the input tables, positionally mapped and represented as Python function arguments. 4return Data the function writes, mapped positionally to destination paths defined on line 7. Each element in the input_tables parameter represents a Tabsdata table to be written to S3 and maps positionally to an argument in the function body. Each value in the function body's return statement maps positionally to an S3 path in the paths parameter, which determines where that table is written in S3. Step 6Register the subscriber into the collection tdk fn register --coll exports --path write_files.py::write_files
documents.s: Write and Register a Subscriber Function

documents.t: Step 7Trigger the subscriber tdk fn trigger --coll exports --name write_files Tabsdata writes one object per path on the server.
Use relative paths in S3Dest(paths=[...]). Destination paths can contain ${EXEC_PLAN_ID}, ${TRX_ID}, and ${EXEC_PLAN_TS}, which are resolved when the subscriber writes the files.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project You can use this built-in Tabsdata subscriber to write tables from the Tabsdata server to Amazon S3 as parquet files and add those files to AWS Glue Iceberg tables.
documents.s: Subscribe data to Iceberg on AWS Glue

documents.t: Here is an example subscriber named write_employees. It reads departments table and multiple employees tables from Tabsdata. Subsequently, it writes the tables to the output HR folder. This subscriber executes automatically as soon as a new commit occurs on any of its input tables. import tabsdata as td s3_credentials = td.S3AccessKeyCredentials( # HashiCorp is a type of secret store, ideal for production use cases. # For rapid testing, you can refer to the credential values directly. You can also use environment variables as detailed here: https://docs.tabsdata.com/latest/guide/secrets_management/env_variables/main.html. aws_access_key_id=td.HashiCorpSecret("path-to-secret","S3_ACCESS_KEY"), aws_secret_access_key=td.HashiCorpSecret("path-to-secret","S3_SECRET_KEY"), ) catalog_definition = { "name": "default", "type": "glue", "client.region": "us-east-1", } @td.subscriber( tables=["departments", "employees_1", "employees_2"], destination=td.S3Destination( [ "s3://opt/hr/departments.parquet", "s3://opt/hr/employees_*.parquet", ], credentials = s3_credentials, region = "us-east-1", catalog = td.AWSGlue( definition=catalog_definition, tables=[ "glue_dbname.table", "glue_dbname.table", "glue_dbname.table", ], credentials = s3_credentials, .... ), ), trigger_by=["<trigger_table1>", "<trigger_table2>"] ), def write_employees(tf1: td.TableFrame, tf2: td.TableFrame, tf3: td.TableFrame): return tf1, tf2, tf3 Where: S3_ACCESS_KEY is the value of your Amazon S3 access key. S3_SECRET_KEY is the value of your Amazon S3 secret key. note After defining the function, you need to register it with a Tabsdata collection and execute it. For more information, see Register a Function and Execute a Function.

The following code uses placeholder values for defining a subscriber to write tables from the Tabsdata server to Amazon S3 as parquet files and add those files to AWS Glue Iceberg tables. import tabsdata as td s3_credentials = td.S3AccessKeyCredentials( aws_access_key_id=td.HashiCorpSecret("path-to-secret","S3_ACCESS_KEY"), aws_secret_access_key=td.HashiCorpSecret("path-to-secret","S3_SECRET_KEY"), ) catalog_definition = { "name": "default", "type": "glue", "client.region": "<region_name>", } @td.subscriber( tables=["<input_table1>", "<input_table2>"], destination=td.S3Destination( ["s3://<path_to_file1>", "s3://<path_to_file2>"], credentials = s3_credentials, region = "<region_name>", catalog = td.AWSGlue( definition = catalog_definition, tables = ["<table_1>","<table_2>"], credentials = s3_credentials, auto_create_at = ["<auto_create_1>","<auto_create_2>"], if_table_exists = "<if_table_exists_append_replace>", partitioned_table = "<partitioned_table_bool>", schema_strategy = "<schema_strategy_update_strict>", ), ), trigger_by=["<trigger_table1>", "<trigger_table2>"]), def <subscriber_name>(<table_frame1>: td.TableFrame, <table_frame2>: td.TableFrame): <function_logic> return <table_frame_output1>, <table_frame_output2> note After defining the function, you need to register it with a Tabsdata collection and execute it. For more information, see Register a Function and Execute a Function. Following properties are defined in the setup code above:
<input_table1>, <input_table2>… are the names of the Tabsdata tables to be written to the external system.

<path_to_files>​ <path_to_file1>, <path_to_file2>… are the full system directory paths to the parquet files to write. Please note files must be Parquet files. You can specify as many file paths as needed. Additionally, you can use the following variables within path to files to make the files unique or identifiable by a Tabsdata ID. e.g. td-iceberg/customers-$EXPORT_TIMESTAMP.parquet as used in this Tabsdata tutorial. Field Description $EXECUTION_ID The execution plan ID. $EXPORT_TIMESTAMP Datetime the function started executing in epoch millis. $FUNCTION_RUN_ID The function run ID. $SCHEDULER_TIMESTAMP Datetime when the scheduler set the function run to running, in epoch millis. $TRIGGER_TIMESTAMP Datetime when the execution plan was triggered, in epoch millis. $TRANSACTION_ID The transaction ID. You can define the destination files in the following ways: File Path To write by file path where the file extension is included as part of the file path, define the destination as follows: destination=td.S3Destination(["s3://<path_to_file1.parquet>","s3://<path_to_file2.parquet>"], s3_credentials), <path_to_file1.parquet>… have the extensions of the file included in the file name as part of the path. File Format To write files by file format where format is declared separately and not in the file name, define the destination as follows: destination=td.S3Destination([ "s3://<path_to_file1_no_extension>", "s3://<path_to_file2_no_extension>", ], s3_credentials, format="parquet"), "<path_to_file1_no_extension>", "<path_to_file2_no_extension>"… don’t have the extension in the file name. The extension to all files is mentioned separately in format property. credentials​ A subscriber needs credentials to write files from Amazon S3. Here the value is defined using a variable s3_credentials. The variable is an object of class S3AccessKeyCredentials with following values. S3_ACCESS_KEY is the value of your Amazon S3 access key. S3_SECRET_KEY is the value of your Amazon S3 secret key. path-to-secret is the name of the default key value store in HashiCorp where the credential values are required to be stored. You can use different ways to store the credentials which are highlighted here in the documentation. region​ <region_name> is where your S3 bucket is located. catalog​ This property is used to define the properties of your catalog. definition​ This property defines the catalog. It is of dictionary format, and matches the pyiceberg catalog definition. The value is simply passed through. tables​ These are the names of the Iceberg tables we want to add the parquet files to. They need to have the same number as the parquet files being created in S3. auto_create_at​ If you don’t specify auto_create_at the table must exist in the Iceberg catalog. If you want the publisher to create the table if it does not exist, in the auto_create_at you have to provide an S3 URI where the entry point of Iceberg metadata of the table will be created. Typically you would put the base path where you write the parquet files. e.g. the path would look like: s3://<path_to_file1>. [Optional] if_table_exists​ This is an optional property to define the strategy to follow when the table already exists. replace will create a new table in Iceberg, overwriting the existing one, and append will append to the existing data in the table. Defaults to append. partitioned_table​ This option indicates that the Iceberg table definition corresponds to a partitioned table. If the Iceberg table is a partitioned table, the subscriber function should return an array of TableFrames with each of those TableFrames containing data for one partition only. It is the responsibility of the user publisher creator to partition the data accordingly before returning it. Partition tables can only be used with already existing (and partitioned) Iceberg tables. auto_create_at is not supported, and when using partition tables the if_table_exists strategy must be append. schema_strategy​ Schema strategy indicates if the schema in iceberg will be modified (augmented) if necessary to be compatible with the parquet files being uploaded. If using strict, the function will fail if the schemas differ. Important Points to note:​ Existing tables in AWS Glue can have their schema updated (augmented) to match the written parquet files. Tables can be automatically created in AWS Glue using Tabsdata table schema. The parquet files are registered with AWS Glue as external files for a table. Future versions will add support for replacing partitions in Iceberg partitioned tables.

A subscriber may receive and return a None value instead of TableFrames. When a subscriber receives a None value instead of a TableFrame it means that the requested table dependency version does not exist. When a subscriber returns a None value instead of a TableFrame it means there is no new data to write to the external system. This helps in avoiding the creation of multiple copies of the same data.
documents.s: None as an input and output

documents.t: <trigger_table1>, <trigger_table2>… are the names of the tables in the Tabsdata server. A new commit to any of these tables triggers the subscriber. All listed trigger tables must exist in the server before registering the subscriber. Defining trigger tables is optional. If you don’t define the trigger_by property, the subscriber will be triggered by any of its input tables. If you define the trigger_by property, then only those tables listed in the property can automatically trigger the subscriber. For more information, see Working with Triggers.
<subscriber_name> is the name for the subscriber that you are configuring.

<function_logic> governs the processing performed by the subscriber. You can specify function logic to be a simple write or to perform additional processing as needed. For more information about the function logic that you can include, see Working with Tables. <table_frame1>, <table_frame2>… are the names for the variables that temporarily store source data for processing. <table_frame_output1>, <table_frame_output2>… are the output from the function that are written to the external system.

This section talks about how Tabsdata handles data drift in the output data for this Subscriber connector. The behaviour depends on how schema_strategy is configured in the subscriber. When schema_strategy=update is configured, the schema gets updated is the new commit from the subscriber has a different schema form the previous versions. When schema_strategy=strict is configured, the subscriber does not modify the existing schema. Any schema changes (added, removed, or modified columns) will cause execution to fail. In this mode, the subscriber function must ensure consistent column definitions across executions e.g., by explicitly specifying the columns to export. Also, this applies only if the subscriber function does not contain schema-dependent logic. If such logic exists, changes in the schema may conflict with the function’s expectations, potentially leading to execution errors outside of the configuration of schema_strategy.

Each element positionally maps to a function argument on line 11. 2input_tables Tabsdata tables function input is read from. Each name maps positionally to a function argument on line 11. 3function arguments Data read from the input tables, positionally mapped and represented as Python function arguments. 4return Data the function writes, mapped positionally to destination paths defined on line 7. Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The BigQuery connector lets a subscriber write Tabsdata tables out to BigQuery. Each entry in tables takes one input table, in order, and writes it to that destination table. Setting one up takes two files and four commands: a connection document, the destination collection that carries it, and the subscriber registered into that collection. What you’ll do Configure a connection to BigQuery Write and Register a Subscriber Function Trigger the subscriber function

The connection holds the URI and the credentials, so the subscriber names destination tables and nothing about where the database is. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type bigquery-bulk-out --file conn-bigquery.yaml The file lands in your working directory. Step 2Fill in the URI and the credentials tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.bigquery:BigQueryDestConn spec: staging: kind: bigQueryGcsLocation apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.bigquery:GCSLocation spec: bucket: 'acme-staging' credentials: kind: gcpJsonCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:GCPJson spec: json: 'secret:{"type":"service_account",...}' base_path: '/bigquery' credentials: kind: gcpJsonCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:GCPJson spec: json: 'secret:{"type":"service_account",...}' staging:GCSLocationrequired credentials:GCPJsonrequired project:stroptional dataset:stroptional Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-bigquery.yaml

A destination collection is created together with its connection, which is why --conn-file is required rather than optional, and why the group is destinations rather than sources. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name warehouse --group destinations --conn-file conn-bigquery.yaml Every subscriber registered in warehouse from now on writes through this one connection. Changing environments means swapping the connection rather than editing the Python file.

Step 5Build the subscriber file locally write_sales.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.bigquery import BigQueryDest @subscriber( destination=BigQueryDest( tables=["vendors", "items"], if_table_exists="replace", schema_evolution="strict", ), input_tables=["sales/vendors", "sales/items"], ) def write_sales( vendors: TableFrameSpec, items: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (vendors, items) Input tables are referenced as collection/table, since a subscriber reads from collections other than its own. A subscriber declares no output_tables: it returns one frame per destination slot, and returning None for a slot writes nothing. Step 6Register the subscriber into the collection tdk fn register --coll warehouse --path write_sales.py::write_sales Re-register after every code change. See Subscribers for the rest of the registration flags.
documents.s: Write and Register a Subscriber Function

documents.t: Step 7Run the subscriber tdk fn trigger --coll warehouse --name write_sales Tabsdata writes one destination table per entry on the server. Step 8Verify the data arrived bq query --use_legacy_sql=false "select * from warehouse.vendors limit 5"
BigQuery table names can be fully qualified or completed from the connection defaults. schema_evolution="update" allows new columns during append-style writes; "strict" rejects schema changes.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The ClickHouse connector is destination-only. It stages Parquet files in cloud storage and then loads them through ClickHouse table functions such as s3() or azureBlobStorage(). The connector currently supports S3, Azure Blob, and GCS staging. Each entry in tables takes one input table, in order, and writes it to that destination table. The connector ships separately from the core package: pip install 'tabsdata[clickhouse]' What you’ll do Configure a connection to ClickHouse Write and Register a Subscriber Function Trigger the subscriber function

The connection holds the server address, the credentials, and a staging block naming the cloud storage the load goes through. Rows reach ClickHouse as Parquet staged in that location rather than row by row, so the staging credentials have to be writable as well as readable. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type clickhouse-bulk-out --file conn-clickhouse.yaml The file lands in your working directory. Step 2Fill in the server, the credentials, and the staging location conn-clickhouse.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.clickhouse:ClickHouseDestConn spec: host: 'clickhouse.internal' port: '8123' secure: 'false' database: 'analytics' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_writer' password: 'secret:example-password' staging: kind: clickHouseS3Location apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.clickhouse:S3Location spec: bucket: 'acme-staging' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE' secret_access_key: 'secret:wJalrXUtnFEMI0EXAMPLEKEY' base_path: '/clickhouse' Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-clickhouse.yaml

A destination collection is created together with its connection, which is why --conn-file is required rather than optional, and why the group is destinations rather than sources. Without an explicit trigger_by, a subscriber runs only on a manual trigger. Add trigger_by=[...] when you need it to run automatically as its input tables get new commits.

If an input table dependency does not exist for a run, the subscriber can receive None instead of a frame. Returning None means there is nothing to write for that output slot, which avoids unnecessary duplicate writes. Neither mode changes the destination table's schema: "replace" truncates the existing rows before inserting, and "append" adds to them without touching what's already there. Either way, the returned frame's columns need to match the table MySQL already has, so column additions, removals, or type changes need a manual migration first.

Before you begin Quickstart a Server or Start a Server Create a Project The Snowflake connector lets a subscriber write Tabsdata tables out to Snowflake. Each entry in tables takes one input table, in order, and writes it to that destination table. Setting one up takes two files and four commands: a connection document, the destination collection that carries it, and the subscriber registered into that collection. What you’ll do Configure a connection to Snowflake Write and Register a Subscriber Function Trigger the subscriber function

The connection holds the URI and the credentials, so the subscriber names destination tables and nothing about where the database is. Step 1Generate a connection template using the CLI tdk connection template --type snowflake-bulk-out --file conn-snowflake.yaml The file lands in your working directory. Step 2Fill in the URI and the credentials tip Click a field to expand its details and highlight where it sits in the file; type your own values to build a file you can copy straight out. Toggle optional fields to add or remove them. Credential fields show a sample value and cannot be edited here. connection.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.snowflake:SnowflakeDestConn spec: account: 'secret:xy12345.us-east-1' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_reader' password: 'secret:example-password' account:strrequired credentials:UserPasswordrequired role:stroptional database:stroptional schema:stroptional warehouse:stroptional stage:stroptional Credentials are written as secret:<value>, a literal secret. The CLI strips the value out of the document before it reaches the server and stores it separately, so the file you keep on disk is the only place the plain value ever appears. Reads return the secret's name, never its value. See Connections for the full syntax. Step 3Validate the filled-in template (optional) tdk connection validate --file conn-snowflake.yaml

A destination collection is created together with its connection, which is why --conn-file is required rather than optional, and why the group is destinations rather than sources. Step 4Create the collection and bind the connection to it tdk collection create --name warehouse --group destinations --conn-file conn-snowflake.yaml Every subscriber registered in warehouse from now on writes through this one connection. Changing environments means swapping the connection rather than editing the Python file.

Step 5Build the subscriber file locally write_sales.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.snowflake import SnowflakeDest @subscriber( destination=SnowflakeDest( tables=["vendors", "items"], if_table_exists="append", ), input_tables=["sales/vendors", "sales/items"], ) def write_sales( vendors: TableFrameSpec, items: TableFrameSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return (vendors, items) Input tables are referenced as collection/table, since a subscriber reads from collections other than its own. A subscriber declares no output_tables: it returns one frame per destination slot, and returning None for a slot writes nothing. Step 6Register the subscriber into the collection tdk fn register --coll warehouse --path write_sales.py::write_sales Re-register after every code change. See Subscribers for the rest of the registration flags.
documents.s: Write and Register a Subscriber Function
